items.text: A contractor sees an ad: "Read every insurance policy in under 10 minutes, full comprehension guaranteed, backed by science." He is about to buy it to get through claim files faster. What does the peer-reviewed literature actually say about this kind of claim?

A. It is probably too good to be true; the 2016 review found a real speed-accuracy trade-off and no support for extreme speed with full comprehension — Rayner, Schotter, Masson, Potter and Treiman (2016) call speed-reading claims like this probably too good to be true, grounded in a documented speed-accuracy trade-off, not a blanket endorsement or a narrow legal-document exception.

A speed-reading app markets itself as removing wasted eye movement by flashing one word at a time (RSVP). Based on the 2016 review, how much of total reading time do eye movements actually account for, and what does the app lose by removing them?

B. No more than about 10 percent of reading time; the app also removes the reader's ability to reread confusing passages, which tends to hurt comprehension — The review states eye movements account for no more than 10 percent of total reading time, so removing them yields limited gains, and RSVP also removes helpful rereading, which tends to reduce comprehension rather than improve it.
A fellow LSAT prepper insists the key to beating the clock on Logical Reasoning is a weekend speed-reading course. What is the best response, grounded in what this track can actually source?

C. Decline; no source opened for this track supports a speed-reading-to-LSAT-score claim, and the better-supported path is drilling argument patterns until they are recognized instantly (a derived inference from expertise research, not a cited LSAT finding) — This track never states a score-gain number and has no source tying speed-reading technique to LSAT performance. The better-supported route is the [DERIVED] chunking/pattern-recognition explanation built on general expertise research, clearly labeled as an inference, not a cited LSAT study.

An experienced restoration estimator sizes up a water-stained ceiling almost instantly and has a rough scope before he even measures. What is the best-supported explanation for this speed, and how should it be labeled given the sources opened this run?

D. Chunking: he recognizes patterns from hundreds of prior jobs almost instantly, a [DERIVED] application of Chase and Simon's 1973 expertise research, not a directly cited claim about restoration estimating — The best-supported account is chunking from repeated exposure, drawn from general expertise research (Chase & Simon 1973) and applied here as an explicitly labeled [DERIVED] inference, not a study that measured restoration estimators directly.
A DFS player claims he reads lineup-building articles at 1,800 words per minute with full retention, crediting a speed-reading app. Given the 2016 review, what is the most likely real explanation?

A. He is likely skimming with strong prior knowledge of DFS content, which can look like fast full comprehension but is not the same thing; the review found such extreme claims probably too good to be true — The review found that people who look like exceptional speed readers are usually skilled skimmers with heavy prior topic knowledge, and that extreme full-comprehension speed claims are probably too good to be true.

You need to decide fast whether a 40-page policy even mentions sewer backup coverage, then later need to decide whether to fight a denial under that exact clause. What does the research say about using the same "skim" pass for both tasks?

B. Skimming is right for the quick yes/no check, but deciding whether to fight a denial needs a careful full read of the exact clause, definitions, and any endorsement, since skimming is built for gist, not for relying on exact wording — The review treats skimming as a real, useful skill for gist but not a substitute for a careful read when exact wording will be relied on, which is exactly the difference between locating a clause and litigating it.

A carrier opens claim negotiations at $9,000 on a loss you scoped and documented at $24,000. You know the $9,000 is lowball. Based on the 1974 Tversky and Kahneman anchoring research, why does that number still matter?

C. Even known-arbitrary numbers pull later estimates toward them (insufficient adjustment); the 1974 wheel-of-fortune study found this held even when subjects were paid for accuracy — Tversky and Kahneman's wheel-of-fortune experiment showed median estimates shifted toward an openly random anchor (25% vs. 45% after seeing 10 vs. 65), and paying for accuracy did not remove the effect, so simply knowing a number is arbitrary does not cancel anchoring.

In a DFS salary-cap game, a player's listed salary pulls your gut sense of his true value toward that number before you've built your own projection. What bias is this, and what is the procedural fix?

D. Anchoring; the fix is building your own independent projection and value number before looking at salary, since the 1974 research shows even knowing a number is arbitrary does not stop its pull — This is anchoring: the salary figure, seen first, pulls the value judgment toward it the same way the wheel-of-fortune number did. The fix is procedural, generating your own number before exposure to the anchor, not willpower.

A dramatic house-fire total loss leads the local news. Afterward, homeowners in the area overestimate how common fire losses are relative to water-damage losses, which actually occur far more often. What mechanism from the 1974 paper explains this, and what is the paper's own parallel example?

A. Availability heuristic; the paper's own parallel example is that seeing one car overturned by the road temporarily raises a person's subjective sense of how common accidents are — This is availability: a vivid, easy-to-recall event inflates its felt frequency. The 1974 paper's own illustration is the overturned-car example, where subjective accident risk rises after a vivid sighting even though the true rate has not changed.

After one 150-to-1 DFS longshot stack wins a major tournament, players start treating extreme-longshot builds as a common path to winning. What has actually changed, according to the availability heuristic?

B. Nothing about the real base rate has changed; only the vividness and recency of that one outcome in memory has increased, inflating its felt frequency — Availability inflates the felt frequency of vivid, recent outcomes without changing the underlying base rate; one dramatic win does not raise the true odds of the build working again.

An adjuster privately decides early that a loss looks like wear-and-tear, then reviews photos mainly looking for evidence that fits that theory while downplaying evidence of a sudden event. What is the governing bias, and what did Wason's 1960 subjects do that illustrates the same pattern?

C. Confirmation bias; Wason's subjects, having guessed a narrow rule for the 2-4-6 task, mostly proposed only triples consistent with their own guess instead of testing triples designed to disconfirm it — This is confirmation bias: once a conclusion is picked, the evidence search itself becomes biased toward supporting it. Wason's subjects showed exactly this by testing only triples that fit their guessed rule rather than trying to disconfirm it.

A trader convinced a stock is undervalued keeps tracking only news and data that supports that view and skips past contradicting data. What single discipline, modeled on what Wason's more successful subjects did differently, would correct this?

D. Deliberately seek out the strongest available evidence against the thesis before adding to the position, the same discipline as testing a triple designed to disconfirm a guessed rule rather than confirm it — Wason's successful subjects were the ones who tested triples designed to break their own hypothesis rather than only confirm it; the trading parallel is deliberately hunting for the strongest disconfirming evidence before committing further.
A colleague says, "Wason's 1960 paper is where he coined the term confirmation bias." Is this the precise, defensible way to describe the study?

A. No; Wason's study is the founding experimental demonstration of the confirming-evidence-seeking behavior, but the exact origin of the two-word term "confirmation bias" is disputed in secondary sources and was not resolved this run — This track opened Wason's 1960 paper directly and treats it as the founding demonstration of the behavior, while explicitly flagging the coinage of the specific two-word label as unresolved and disputed, per the domain doc's Traps section.

A GC has already spent $6,000 in staff time and legal letters fighting a carrier over a $3,000 disputed line item, and keeps escalating mainly because of how much has already been spent. What did Arkes and Blumer's 1985 ski-trip experiment show about this exact pattern, and what should the decision be based on instead?

B. A majority of their subjects (33 of 61) chose a worse option because of a larger already-spent cost; the decision here should be based only on the cost to finish the fight versus what remains to be won, not on the $6,000 already spent — In the ski-trip experiment, 33 of the subjects chose the worse, already-paid-for Michigan trip over the better, cheaper Wisconsin trip; the sunk cost should not factor into a forward-looking decision, which should weigh only remaining cost against remaining expected recovery.

A trader refuses to exit a losing position because of how much money is already committed, even though nothing about the current setup still supports the trade. Per Arkes and Blumer's stated explanation for the sunk cost effect, what psychological motive is most likely driving this?

C. The desire not to "appear wasteful" by abandoning an investment already made, the motive Arkes and Blumer identify as the psychological justification for the sunk cost effect — Arkes and Blumer's own account of the sunk cost effect's psychological justification is the desire not to appear wasteful, separate from overconfidence, which the same 1974 Tversky and Kahneman paper treats as a distinct bias (the illusion of validity).

A public adjuster hears one dramatic story about a carrier litigating a bad-faith denial and starts treating litigated bad faith as a common outcome of any denial, even though the real share of denials that ever reach litigated bad faith is low. Which 1974 finding does this resemble most closely, and what corrects it?

D. The Dick/engineer-lawyer demonstration of base-rate neglect; the fix is asking what the actual base rate of litigated bad-faith outcomes is before reacting to one vivid case — This is base-rate neglect: a vivid, specific case overrides the actual background frequency, the same error subjects showed when they ignored the explicitly stated 70/30 or 30/70 engineer-lawyer base rate for an uninformative description.

A running back posts a 40-point fantasy outing off an unusual game script, and a DFS player starts treating that single game as representative of the player's normal output. What does base-rate neglect say is being ignored?

A. The player's actual season-long per-touch and target-share base rate, which is the better predictor of next week's expected points than one vivid outlier game — Base-rate neglect means a vivid, specific case (the 40-point outlier) crowds out the more reliable season-long base rate, which remains the better predictor going forward.

An estimator feels very confident in a scope-and-price number because the damage pattern looks clean and consistent (one obvious water line, one obvious source). Per the 1974 paper's "illusion of validity," what should actually temper that confidence?

B. How often that kind of clean pattern-match has actually held up once demolition revealed hidden moisture or a second cause, since confidence tracks how good the story looks, not real predictive reliability — The illusion of validity is unwarranted confidence produced by a good fit between the story and the input data; the 1974 paper's own flight-instructor example shows a clean-feeling causal story can be entirely wrong, so confidence should be checked against actual track record, not story quality.

A bettor feels very confident in a model's pick because the model's explanation for why the team covers fits together neatly. What does the illusion of validity say this confidence should actually be checked against?

C. The model's real track record of being right on similar picks in the past, not how neatly the current explanation fits together — A neat-fitting narrative is exactly the illusion of validity at work; real confidence should be calibrated against the model's actual historical accuracy, not the feeling produced by an internally consistent story.

A trader just had one huge, vivid winning trade and now sizes new trades more aggressively because "big wins happen more than people think," while in the same week refusing to close an old losing position because of how much money is already committed to it. Which two biases are at work, in order?

C. Availability heuristic (the vivid recent win inflates its felt frequency), then sunk cost fallacy (the already-committed money, not the position's current merit, is driving the hold) — The first behavior is availability: a vivid, recent outcome inflates its felt frequency without changing the real base rate. The second is sunk cost: the decision to hold is being driven by money already committed rather than the position's current expected value.
